# Exact all-index primitive and coefficient generator

## Scope and definitions

Let integers m>=k>=2 be fixed, let 0<p<1, and put

    b=(k+p-1)/m,
    P_(k,m)(p)=Pr(Gamma(k,1)+p Exp(1)
                     >=Exp(1)+b Gamma(m,1)),

with independent random variables. This note proves exact algebraic
formulas valid for every such k,m. It does not assert the conjectured
coefficient-sign pattern of the final polynomial or an endpoint
minimum theorem for arbitrary k.

Write

    q=k-1,       c=1-p,       C=p+q,
    A=q+(m+1)p,  B=m+p+q,
    D=q p^2+[(k+1)m+k^2-k+2]p+q(m+k+1).               (1)

D has strictly positive coefficients. Define a polynomial F_(k,m)
by the finite coefficient extraction

    F_(k,m)(p)=[z^q]
      (1+2Bc z)/[(1+Bc z)(1-2pB z)^2
                              (1+2cC z)^(m+1)].       (2)

The symbol [z^q] denotes the coefficient in the formal power series
at z=0; only its first q+1 coefficients are needed. This is a
finite algebraic definition, with no analytic convergence issue.

## 1. Independent derivation from the actual density

Let T be the sum of the fractional positive's unit exponential
and the Gamma(m) variable, and let U be that exponential divided
by T. Their gamma change of variables gives independent laws
T~Gamma(m+1,1), U~Beta(1,m). If W=Gamma(k,1)-Exp(1), independent
of T,U, and Z=W/T, then

    P_(k,m)(p)=Pr(Z>=b)
      +integral_(-p)^b [(p+z)/(p+b)]^m f_Z(z) dz.       (3)

Direct exponential convolution gives

    f_W(w)=2^(-k)e^w                         for w<0,
    f_W(w)=2^(-k)e^(-w)
                       sum_(j=0)^q (2w)^j/j!         for w>=0.

For example, for w>=0 expand (w+t)^(k-1) in the convolution
integral against e^(-2t). Integrating t^ell e^(-2t) gives exactly
the displayed coefficients; the negative side is the gamma
Laplace transform at one.

Integrating T f_W(zT) against the Gamma(m+1) density now yields

    f_Z(z)=(m+1)2^(-k)(1-z)^(-m-2)                    for z<0,
    f_Z(z)=(m+1)2^(-k) sum_(j=0)^q
           2^j binom(m+j+1,j) z^j/(1+z)^(m+j+2)      for z>=0. (4)

These are finite rational expressions on their respective
half-lines, including their matching values at zero.

Differentiate (3). The two upper boundary terms cancel; the
lower boundary term is zero. On compact subintervals of p>0 the
integrands and their derivatives are bounded on the finite moving
integration ranges, which justifies this differentiation. One gets

    P'_(k,m)(p)=J(p)/(p+b)^(m+1),
    J(p)=integral_(-p)^b (p+z)^(m-1)
                         [q-(m+1)z] f_Z(z) dz.        (5)

## 2. The exact negative part and positive primitive

The substitution u=(p+z)/(1-z) on [-p,0] gives the negative part

    J_-(p)=2^(-k) p^m[(m+1)q+(mk+1)p]/[m(1+p)^2].    (6)

On the positive range use t=(p+z)/(1+z), with endpoints p and

    T_*=A/B.

Define

    S(t)=sum_(j=0)^q 2^j binom(m+j+1,j)
                              (t-p)^j c^(q-j),
    G(t)=[A-(m+k)t]S(t).

If G(t)=sum_(ell=0)^k g_ell t^ell, define

    Q(t)=sum_(ell=0)^k g_ell t^ell/(m+ell).

Then (t^m Q(t))'=t^(m-1)G(t), and the exact transformed integral is

    J_+(p)=(m+1)/[2^k c^(k+1)]
                     [T_*^m Q(T_*)-p^m Q(p)].         (7)

The transformation can also be checked termwise directly in (4):
its j-th summand becomes

    (m+1)2^(-k)c^(-j-2)
       t^(m-1)(t-p)^j[A-(m+k)t],dt.

Thus all powers of c and both moving endpoints in (7) are fixed
by the actual density, rather than by interpolation from small k.

## 3. Uniform lower-endpoint cancellation

Set

    V_0=q(m+1)+(m+1-mq)p,
    N_0=(m+1)q+(mk+1)p,
    r=-2p,       s=c.

Beta integration of the polynomial primitive at its lower endpoint
gives the finite identity

    m(m+1)Q(p)=sum_(j=0)^q r^j s^(q-j)[V_0+jA].       (8)

Indeed the two required integrals after t=pu are

    integral_0^1 u^(m-1)(1-u)^j du
      =(m-1)!j!/(m+j)!,
    integral_0^1 u^m(1-u)^j du
      =m!j!/(m+j+1)!.

Multiplication by 2^j binom(m+j+1,j) cancels their factorials
and yields exactly the linear factor V_0+jA in (8).

The two finite geometric sums are

    sum_(j=0)^q r^j s^(q-j)=(s^k-r^k)/(s-r),
    sum_(j=0)^q j r^j s^(q-j)
      =[r s^k-k s r^k+(k-1)r^(k+1)]/(s-r)^2.

Their denominators s-r=1+p are positive. Direct multiplication
gives two polynomial identities:

    V_0(s-r)+Ar=N_0 s,
    V_0(s-r)+A[k s-(k-1)r]=D.                         (9)

Substituting (8)--(9) into (6)--(7) cancels the whole s^k term.
The remaining lower-endpoint contribution is exactly

    J_-(p)-(m+1)p^m Q(p)/[2^k c^(k+1)]
       =(-1)^k p^(m+k)D/[m c^(k+1)(1+p)^2].           (10)

This proves the cancellation simultaneously for arbitrary k,m.

## 4. The upper endpoint and its rational generator

Write S(t)=sum_(ell=0)^q S_ell t^ell. Expanding its definition gives

    S_ell=sum_(j=ell)^q 2^j binom(m+j+1,j) binom(j,ell)
                                      (-p)^(j-ell)c^(q-j).       (11)

At T_*=A/B, termwise integration yields

    Q(T_*)=A sum_(ell=0)^q S_ell A^ell/B^(ell+1)
                   *[A-ell c]/[(m+ell)(m+ell+1)].     (12)

To check (12), integrate A t^(m+ell-1)-(m+k)t^(m+ell).
The remaining numerator is
[(m+ell+1)B-(m+k)(m+ell)]=A-ell c.
For ell=0 it has a second factor A; for ell>=1 the factor
A^(ell+1) already contains A^2. Thus

    F_(k,m)=(-1)^q m(m+1) B^k Q(T_*)/A^2              (13)

is a polynomial in p of degree at most 2q. There is no division
by a root in this polynomial assertion: the factor A^2 cancels
term by term in (12).

Here is a derivation of the compact coefficient formula (2).
In (11) put j=ell+r. The factorial identity

    m(m+1) 2^ell binom(m+ell+1,ell)
                    /[(m+ell)(m+ell+1)]
       =2^ell binom(m+ell-1,ell)

turns (12)--(13) into a nested binomial sum. Temporarily regard
A,B,c,p as independent constants, sum that expression over its
outer degree q, and use

    sum_(ell>=0) binom(m+ell-1,ell)y^ell=(1-y)^(-m),
    sum_(ell>=0) ell binom(m+ell-1,ell)y^ell
                                         =my(1-y)^(-m-1).

The resulting formal generating function before the factor
(-1)^q is

    [1+2(pB-A-mc)z]/
       [(1-Bc z)(1+2pB z)^2(1+2(pB-A)z)^(m+1)].       (14)

All rearrangements are identities of formal power series, whose
coefficient of any fixed degree receives only finitely many terms.
Now specialize A,B,c from (1). The two exact relations

    pB-A=-c(p+q)=-cC,
    pB-A-mc=-cB

simplify (14). Replacing z by -z supplies its factor (-1)^q and
gives exactly (2). This proves that coefficient formula rather
than merely defining an empirically matching sequence.

In particular, at p=1 the factors containing c disappear, and

    F_(k,m)(1)=k 2^(k-1)(m+k)^(k-1)>0.                (15)

## 5. Exact derivative numerator and universal log-ratio factor

Equations (7), (10), and (13) give

    J(p)=(-1)^k
      [2^k p^(m+k)B^(m+k)D
                  -(1+p)^2 A^(m+2)F_(k,m)(p)]
       /[2^k m c^(k+1)(1+p)^2 B^(m+k)].              (16)

This identity is valid for every 0<p<1 and retains all signs.
Where F_(k,m)>0, define the positive ratio

    R(p)=2^k p^(m+k)B^(m+k)D/
                    [(1+p)^2 A^(m+2)F_(k,m)(p)].      (17)

Its logarithmic derivative is

    R'/R=(m+k)/p+(m+k)/B-(m+2)(m+1)/A
                         +D'/D-2/(1+p)-F'/F.         (18)

After multiplication by p(1+p)BA D F, the numerator is the
explicit polynomial

    L=DF[(m+k)(1+p)BA+(m+k)p(1+p)A
             -(m+2)(m+1)p(1+p)B-2pBA]
                  +p(1+p)BA(D'F-DF').                (19)

Its degree is at most 2k+3. It is divisible by (p-1)^k, so

    K_(k,m)(p)=L/(p-1)^k                              (20)

is a polynomial of degree at most k+3. This divisibility has a
proof independent of any small-k symbolic computation. The
actual integral (5), split at zero, is real analytic in p in a
neighborhood of 1: its finite rational integrands have no pole
on their moving intervals. Therefore the numerator of (16)
vanishes to order at least k+1 at p=1. By (15), the denominator
factor used to define R is nonzero there. Hence R-1 vanishes to
order at least k+1, and R'/R vanishes to order at least k.
The factor clearing (18) is nonzero at 1. Thus L has the claimed
polynomial factor, proving (20).

## 6. What is proved and what is not

Equations (2), (10), (13), (16), and (19)--(20) are proved
all-index identities, derived from the density rather than from
symbolic pattern fitting. They provide an exact finite coefficient
generator for any subsequent sign argument.

The conjectural uniform coefficient pattern for K is negative
constant and linear coefficients, an unrestricted quadratic
coefficient, and positive higher coefficients for m>=k. Exact
checks for finitely many parameters support it, but no proof of
that assertion is supplied or used here. The sign hunt is paused;
this source does not claim an all-k endpoint theorem or completion
of the low-maximum angular estimate.
